I was talking a mile a minute, just non-stop, telling my husband about all these grand plans I had to reorganize the entire garage, the basement, the attic—which we don't even use—and I just felt this overwhelming, intense drive to fix absolutely everything in the house. I was painting the trim in the living room at three in the morning, and I was so sure I was doing the most important work of my life. 

And that's... that's exactly when I started hearing it. While I was in the middle of all that endless energy, that's when my name started being called from the hallway or at the warehouse. It was during that exact time. But before that? Never. I'd never heard a thing out of the ordinary in my forty-eight years on this earth. And then, well, after that high-energy phase kind of crashed, and I fell into this really awful, dark, withdrawn period where I couldn't even get out of bed to face the day... the voice stopped. I haven't heard it since I got so low and quiet. It's like it only existed when my brain was running at a hundred miles an hour, and once I shut down, the voice shut down too. So, no, it's not all the time, just... just during that one really wild stretch.

But by the time Monday actually rolled around, that intense energy had already started to sort of... leak out of me, I guess. I really think if that phase had lasted even one more day, though, I would have drained the joint checking account on craft supplies we have absolutely no room for. But no, no real damage done, just a lot of talk.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes. Honestly, sad almost feels like too small of a word for it, if that makes sense. After all that running around and arguing with my husband over the laptop and the resin supplies, and all that endless buzzing energy I had... it just vanished. It was like someone just yanked the power cord right out of the wall. 

And when it went, I just... I dropped into this heavy, empty feeling. It's so hard to explain because it wasn't like I was crying because I was upset about the business plan not working out, or because I was mad at my husband anymore. It was just this profound, crushing emptiness. I would go and sit at that exact same kitchen table—the very same one where I was writing out my grand master plans on the back of the grocery receipts just a few days before—and I would just sit there and cry over absolutely nothing. I mean, nothing at all. 

The tears would just fall, and my husband would come into the kitchen and see me, and he'd ask what was wrong, and I couldn't even give him a reason. I didn't have one. I just felt like... like I couldn't get myself back. The woman who was ready to march into Gary's office and quit was gone, but the normal me, the one who just puts on her safety vest and goes to the warehouse and does her job, she was gone too. I was just this heavy shell sitting there, staring at the wood grain on the table, crying into my coffee mug for hours on end. It felt like I was wearing a lead apron, you know, the kind they put over your chest at the dentist for x-rays? Just so heavy. No, never. Honestly, I think that's why it was so... so completely bizarre for both of us. My husband and I, I mean. I have never in my life felt anything even remotely close to that before.

That's my normal. That's how I've been for as long as I can remember. 

So to suddenly be up all night, buzzing like a refrigerator, feeling like I didn't need to sleep at all, and planning to take over the entire craft world with epoxy resin... it was completely out of left field. My husband was just totally thrown by it. He kept looking at me and asking, "Who are you right now? What has gotten into you?" because in the twenty-odd years we've been together, he has never, ever seen me act like that.

I've always been the practical one, the one worrying about how we're going to pay the electric bill, not the one writing crazy business plans on the back of the envelope it came in. So, no, nothing like that before this past time. This was the very first time anything like that has ever happened to me, and it just... looking back on it now from this awful, heavy place I'm in, it really scares me. It's like I was a completely different person for that week, just some stranger living in my house, using my laptop, ready to throw away my job and my savings. It's just the sound that's playing tricks on me, nothing else.\n\nDoctor: Do you hear your name being called all the time, or does it happen at specific times or intervals?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it's not all the time, thank goodness, because I don't think I could survive if it was every single minute of the day. Looking back on it now, it really only started up during that... that really intense stretch I had a little while ago. \n\nYou see, for about a week or so, I was just... I was completely wired. I don't even know how else to explain it. I was barely sleeping, maybe an hour or two a night, if that, but I wasn't tired at all. I was practically buzzing. I was talking a mile a minute, just non-stop, telling my husband about all these grand plans I had to reorganize the entire garage, the basement, the attic—which we don't even use—and I just felt this overwhelming, intense drive to fix absolutely everything in the house. I was painting the trim in the living room at three in the morning, and I was so sure I was doing the most important work of my life. \n\nAnd that's... that's exactly when I started hearing it. While I was in the middle of all that endless energy, that's when my name started being called from the hallway or at the warehouse. It was during that exact time. But before that? Never. I'd never heard a thing out of the ordinary in my forty-eight years on this earth. And then, well, after that high-energy phase kind of crashed, and I fell into this really awful, dark, withdrawn period where I couldn't even get out of bed to face the day... the voice stopped. I haven't heard it since I got so low and quiet. It's like it only existed when my brain was running at a hundred miles an hour, and once I shut down, the voice shut down too. So, no, it's not all the time, just... just during that one really wild stretch.\n\nDoctor: During that week when you were barely sleeping and had all that energy, did you feel like you were on top of the world, invincible, or unusually confident?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. Usually, I'm just, you know, punching the clock at the warehouse, putting my head down, doing my job, paying the bills. But that week... oh my lord, I was just bursting with these huge, incredible ideas. \n\nI do a little bit of crafting on the side, mostly resin work, like coasters and little decorative trays with dried flowers in them, and some knitting when my hands aren't too cramped up from pulling stock all shift. Usually it's just a hobby, just for me or for birthday gifts for my nieces, nothing serious. But right then, during that stretch where I wasn't sleeping and had all that energy? I got it in my head that I was an absolute genius. I was completely convinced that I could turn my crafts into a real retirement business, and not just eventually, but right away. \n\nI remember I was sitting at the kitchen table at maybe three or four in the morning, just buzzing, writing out this massive, elaborate business plan on the back of our electric bills and grocery receipts. I was talking a mile a minute to my husband—who was just standing there in his pajamas begging me to please just come to bed—telling him that I was going to quit the warehouse, open a fancy storefront downtown, and that we were going to be practically rich overnight. I just knew it in my bones. I felt so incredibly smart, like everyone would see I had figured out the perfect plan for our family. I honestly thought people would be lining up down the block for my little resin coasters and that I was about to be some famous entrepreneur. Looking back on it now, it's a little embarrassing because I'm not a business person, I'm an order filler, but in that moment, I really believed I was untouchable and that I had all the answers to everything.\n\nDoctor: Did you make any impulsive decisions or purchases during that week when you had all the energy and felt invincible?\n\nPatient: Well, no, surprisingly. I had my online shopping cart just completely loaded up. I was ready to drop at least two thousand dollars right then and there. I had the credit card out of my purse and everything.\n\nBut... well, my husband, he's a very practical man, and he saw what I was doing. I fully intended to march into the supervisor's office first thing Monday morning—Gary is his name, he's been the floor manager for twelve years and he's a real stickler for attendance, always breathing down our necks about scan rates—and I was going to march right in there, slam my safety vest on his desk, and tell him I was moving on to bigger and better things. \n\nBut by the time Monday actually rolled around, that intense energy had already started to sort of... leak out of me, I guess. No... no, I really haven't. Just like that crazy buzzing energy, this heavy, awful feeling is completely new territory for me. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, I've had bad days before. You work on concrete floors for ten hours a day, pulling orders and dealing with a manager like Gary riding you about your pick rates, and you're going to have days where you come home and you just want to cry from sheer exhaustion. So, no, never. Before this whole nightmare started a few months ago, I had never experienced anything even close to this dark place. It’s like my brain just broke after all that wild energy ran out, and I don't know how to fix it, because I've never had to deal with anything like this in my entire life. I've always been a fighter, you know? A hard worker who just gets the job done. And now I just feel like I'm completely hollowed out, and it's just so terrifying because I don't have any past experience to draw on to figure out how to climb out of it.

I was completely convinced that I could turn my crafts into a real retirement business, and not just eventually, but right away. \n\nI remember I was sitting at the kitchen table at maybe three or four in the morning, just buzzing, writing out this massive, elaborate business plan on the back of our electric bills and grocery receipts. I was talking a mile a minute to my husband—who was just standing there in his pajamas begging me to please just come to bed—telling him that I was going to quit the warehouse, open a fancy storefront downtown, and that we were going to be practically rich overnight. I just knew it in my bones. I felt so incredibly smart, like everyone would see I had figured out the perfect plan for our family. I honestly thought people would be lining up down the block for my little resin coasters and that I was about to be some famous entrepreneur. Looking back on it now, it's a little embarrassing because I'm not a business person, I'm an order filler, but in that moment, I really believed I was untouchable and that I had all the answers to everything.\n\nDoctor: Did you make any impulsive decisions or purchases during that week when you had all the energy and felt invincible?\n\nPatient: Well, no, surprisingly. I mean, I really, really wanted to, don't get me wrong. I had my laptop open on the kitchen counter—right next to all those electric bills and receipts I was writing my master plan on—and I must have had about fifty different tabs open on the browser. \n\nI was looking at bulk suppliers for epoxy resin, you know, the industrial two-part kind that you have to mix perfectly or it gets all cloudy and ruins the whole batch? I had my online shopping cart just completely loaded up. I'm talking gallons of the stuff, plus all these intricate silicone molds, the big ones for making tiered cake stands and serving trays, and enough gold leaf and mica powder to cover the entire warehouse floor where I work. I was ready to drop at least two thousand dollars right then and there. I had the credit card out of my purse and everything.\n\nBut... well, my husband, he's a very practical man, and he saw what I was doing. He actually came over, put his hand over mine, and gently closed the laptop screen. Oh, I was so mad at him in that moment! I really was. I told him he was stifling my creativity, that he just didn't have the vision, and that he was ruining our one big chance at early retirement. We bickered about it for a good hour while he was just trying to get me to drink a glass of water and go to sleep. But honestly, thank goodness for him, because I never actually clicked 'checkout' on any of it. \n\nAnd as for decisions, like I said before, I *told* him I was going to quit my job. I fully intended to march into the supervisor's office first thing Monday morning—Gary is his name, he's been the floor manager for twelve years and he's a real stickler for attendance, always breathing down our necks about scan rates—and I was going to march right in there, slam my safety vest on his desk, and tell him I was moving on to bigger and better things. \n\nBut by the time Monday actually rolled around, that intense energy had already started to sort of... leak out of me, I guess. I was still feeling restless, but the grand ideas were fading, and I didn't actually go through with it. I just put my vest on and clocked in like normal, even though I was starting to feel completely exhausted from not sleeping. So, no, I didn't actually spend our savings or throw away my job, thank heavens. I just made a whole lot of noise about doing it. I really think if that phase had lasted even one more day, though, I would have drained the joint checking account on craft supplies we have absolutely no room for. But no, no real damage done, just a lot of talk.\n\nDoctor: When you fell into that really awful, dark, withdrawn period after your energy crashed, did you feel sad or hopeless most of the time?\n\nPatient: Well, yes. Honestly, sad almost feels like too small of a word for it, if that makes sense. After all that running around and arguing with my husband over the laptop and the resin supplies, and all that endless buzzing energy I had... it just vanished. It was like someone just yanked the power cord right out of the wall. \n\nAnd when it went, I just... I dropped into this heavy, empty feeling. It's so hard to explain because it wasn't like I was crying because I was upset about the business plan not working out, or because I was mad at my husband anymore. It was just this profound, crushing emptiness. I would go and sit at that exact same kitchen table—the very same one where I was writing out my grand master plans on the back of the grocery receipts just a few days before—and I would just sit there and cry over absolutely nothing. I was just this heavy shell sitting there, staring at the wood grain on the table, crying into my coffee mug for hours on end. I kept wishing I could figure out how to just be myself again, but I was just stuck in that dark, empty place.\n\nDoctor: How long did that heavy, empty feeling last after your energy crashed?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, it's still there. How am I going to put my steel-toe boots on and go pull stock for an entire shift? \n\nIt's been exactly like that ever since that big crash. Just three months of this awful, dark cloud following me into the warehouse, following me down the aisles, following me back home, and sitting right there next to me at the kitchen table. Well, like I was saying just a minute ago... no, never before this recent time. This one time, this past episode, was the very first and only time I've ever felt anything like that.
